newsitem.title: DUBAI: Saudi defence minister's London talks not on arms.
newsitem.headline: Saudi defence minister's London talks not on arms.

text.p: Saudi Arabia's Defence Minister Prince Sultan will travel to London on Wednesday for talks that will cover a wide range of issues but will not focus on arms sales, a British embassy official in Riyadh said on Tuesday.
He said the two-day visit was the first official one to Britain by a senior Saudi prince since Prince Sultan held talks there in 1989.

"The talks will cover a wide range of issues. We don't expect defence sales to figure highly in the talks. They will not be the focus of the visit," the official told Reuters by telephone from the Saudi capital.
Prince Sultan, who is visiting Britain in his capacity as second deputy prime minister, will be accompanied by senior government and military officials.

British officials on visits to Saudi Arabia have been rallying support for British main battle tank (MBT) maker Vickers Plc, competing with French and U.S. companies to supply up to 200 MBTs to the kingdom.
Saudi Arabia, the world's biggest arms purchaser, has not indicated when it will place an order.

In the mid-1980s Riyadh turned to London for its defence needs after receiving a rejection from Washington. Saudi Arabia eventually awarded Britain two major oil-for-arms deals worth more than $20 billion for Tornado, Hawk and PC-9 aircraft, specialised naval vessels and other hardware and services.
Since then the two countries have concluded arms deals worth more than $30 billion for a variety of sophisticated weapons including ships and aircraft.

Britain's relations with the world's largest oil producer and exporter has suffered tensions, coupled with veiled Saudi threats that London might lose some lucrative contracts because of bitter criticism of the Saudi royal family by London-based Saudi dissident Mohammad al-Masari.

Both Saudi and British officials say the two countries have now overcome the tensions. British officials said the Saudi government understood that Britain had done its best to curb Masari and had been barred from deporting him by its own laws.
Diplomats did not expect Masari to be discussed during Prince Sultan's visit, his third trip to a key Western ally after talks in the United States and France in the past month.
The embassy official said Prince Sultan would meet Prime Minister John Major and several other ministers, including the commerce and defence secretaries.
He would also call on Queen Elisabeth.
His discussions with the government would centre on ways of boosting trade and investment between the two countries, British relations with Saudi Arabia and the Middle East peace process.
The British embassy said the value of British investments in Saudi Arabia was $2 billion and trade between the two countries in 1996 was worth 2.4 billion pounds ($3.84 billion).
